blocks.x: All right, Johnny Deidroy, take 378. No. Give me your name again, Johnny. The correct pronunciation.
Well, the correct pronunciation is De-Draw.
De-Draw.
Johnny De-Draw. Better known as Johnny De-Droy, and sometimes Johnny De-Troy.

And it didn't register before, so I'll put the date down again. We're here at the Howard Tilt Memorial Library, the Jazz Archive, March the 16th, is right? Yes. In 1973. And your name? Dexter Thompson. And my name is Dick Allen. So, since the machine didn't work before, let's try and see if you can answer that question again as well.
It was perfect. I'm with you. Help yourself.
Okay. The question was what, about your first band?

I organized my band in 1917. The play at a hotel in Atlantic City. When the war came on, the contract was cancelled. So I played a little jazz at the Orphan Theater, and Mr. Grunlong happened to be in the audience, and he heard us. He waited for me, and he said, they tell me you have a band. I said, yes. He said, could I hear it? I said, let's play him. So we made an audition. We played two numbers. He okayed the orchestra, sent us to get uniforms, and we stayed with him four solid years in the cave and in the forest grill. Forest Grill was on Barone Street. The cave was under the Roosevelt. Then the Roosevelt was then called the Grunlong. We finished at the Grunlong, now the Roosevelt, on the 19th of March and opened at Cobb's Restaurant on St. Charles Street on the 21st. One day, because Mr. Cobb had been after me for a couple of years, we stayed with Mr. Cobb seven years. And like all good things, let's come to an end. During the period at Cobb, we made records for the Oak Cave phonograph company. The personnel of the orchestra changed from time to time, as it does with all bands, but I managed to give them the kind of music they want. And then, we had a good job. Our strong point was good Dixieland, clean Dixieland, and show tunes. Because having had good musicians, we could play anything. And we had the best people in the town, and some of them liked good music now and then. Through that engagement, I signed a five-year contract with O.K. O.K. went on for business, so I had made a few dollars on the record, so I didn't worry about it. In addition to that, Mr. Cobb gave me the music for the luncheon period, the dinner period, and I had the dance man. In addition to that, I was finishing the music at three Morrisons cafeterias. Strange to say they had music. As soon as AFSCAP demanded a license for every seat, they cut out the music.
Progress.
No, that's progress. Now what, now what, you can't shut it off now? That's the first answer.
Sure, but I want to ask you one question. Yes, we can. What about Mr. Grunwald? Did he play an instrument?

Mr. Grunwald was a very capable piano player, but he would only do it around us, because he was a big man. The Grunwald Music Store was named after Mr. Grunwald. I said to Louis a while ago, if I was a mistake, his name was Theodore, Theodore Grunwald. He was a fine musician and you couldn't fool him. He knew music, and he knew musicians when he heard of him. He was great on intonation, and that's what we had. When we played, we played in tune. That's what made our jazz just a little bit better than the other so-called jazz, because the musicians, they were not schooled. I doubt it sometimes that they didn't tune.
Adjusted as they went along.

We were supreme for, I'll say, the other bands that made maybe perhaps a greater reputation, because they left town. But we stayed in New Orleans and made a living. And even sent the recording outfit to New Orleans to record my orchestra and other local orchestras. And the recordings were not good because they didn't demand that they sent. He was more intent on having a good time than he was making good records. But the records I made in New York in the studio, well, they were made properly. Well, naturally all the good things come to an end. I moved over. I took over the St. Charles Orchestra, St. Charles Theatre, who was playing stock. And Mr. Garinger, who was the general manager, happened to be over in Biloxi. Incidentally, I had an arrangement with Mr. Cobb and the manager of the White House in Biloxi that I would play for Cobb in the winter and play for the White House in the summer, which meant fishing and golf and good times. And Garinger happened to be over there. And he said, Johnny, you have a fine orchestra. I said, thank you, Mr. Garinger. I said, you know, that's just the orchestra you need in the pit at the St. Charles. He said, that's an idea. Come see me. I come see him. He gave me a contract for two years. And all we did was play between the acts. And that was the reason we got out of those funny uniforms you saw in the picture. We couldn't change quick enough to start at 11 o'clock at the Rosebud, because sometimes the show would run late. So we wore tuxedos. And it was the first Dictionary Band ever to wear a tuxedo. And my boys, they liked the dress. They were young. They made a fine appearance. I was the oldest in the band. And the girls naturally liked them. They knew every party. And when we moved into the Grill, which was really for the younger people and collegiates, You didn't have to spend as much money on the grill, you could order what you want. We found out that we drank R&J, which raised the price to ninety cents, you know, to get together, get a dollar. And we got to know it as the Grill Band more than any other name, the Grill Band. Everybody knew the Grill Band. And then we were smart, we played for benefits and things, and we played for bond drives. And I think I was pretty smart, but keeping the band up, up, up, up, never did let it go. I was considered pretty hard, but I wasn't. I just wanted the music to play properly, wanted the musicians to act like musicians in the middle of the day. And that's how it started. I think that's the reason why I had some success. But I always hired good men. Like one time I said to my bassist, who was one of the best in town, I won't mention his name, I said, you know I'm fortunate to have a bass man like you. Well he says, frankly, Johnny I'm playing with you because you get plenty of work. Realize there's no feeling there. So why should I show all the feeling? Play right. Look good. Act like a gentleman. That's all. That's all I ask. And come on time. No smoking on the stand. I was taught that lesson when I played at the convention at the Ishwater. The manager says, I knew it wasn't your band. He says, it didn't sound like your band and they're all smoking up there. And I said, oh this guy doesn't like smoking. So I thought about no smoking on the bandstand. And from then on that was the rule. It might have been a hardship. And if it came to a point, you'd rather have the cigarettes than the money, I'll get me another man. That's all. That's all I can tell you about. Now when I organized my band, Dixieland was the thing. Everything was Dixieland, but we did play a lot of show tunes and pretty tunes and we played some slow music because the younger people, some of them liked to dance to slow tunes. But we were getting more to people that could afford the Grinnell Hotel than the College Boys, because after I moved to Cobbs, Friday night got to be known as College Night, and we had all the young kids, but we had to take everything off the table. You couldn't leave an ashtray on the table or a tablecloth because we'd go out with the kids. But they were my success. Then we got to, it was so well known that my band used to play with the Tulane Band. They had a terrible band at that time. We would help them out, you know. Then we'd play, we'd see the game, we'd go out to the school. We didn't go many places. We went to Baton Rouge because it was a dollar round trip and something like that. But it made business. It helped. It really did help. Now, do you want to shut that off while I read this next one?
What was the question? I'm lost.

The question is, was there much attempt on part of white, legitimate musicians to play in a Negro style? Well there's no doubt that the white musicians who could play were influenced by their style. But to my positive knowledge, the Negro musicians didn't seem to have the schooling or the technique that the musicians had before they started to play jazz, you see? And that gave us a chance to perhaps improve or modernize in those days their style of music. But their music was always good. And I used to take a leaf out of Satchmo's book when I realized that he wasn't playing 32 bars in a whole number sometimes. And then I'd be out there blowing my head off and getting a tired lip, I found out how to distribute it. I learned, I learned. And the later years you'd notice that Louis Armstrong didn't play much more than 16 bars. He could play, but he wasn't bodily well. You know, Louis wasn't, and he's gone. And I'm frank enough to say that I didn't think it's wrong to copy some of his choruses. Because his clean style was the style that I liked. He didn't play that wild jazz. I had all these records, and Dutch Andrus, who had a little store on Oak Street, used to collect for me, all the Louis Armstrong records we could find, I gave them the lowest ten cents a piece. But I had a calamity, my granddaughter knocked them off the table and said, okay, okay. And I loved those records. I wouldn't have applauded with them at any price because his chorus only misbehaved and stuff like that, simply great. So there's no doubt that the colored musicians influenced the white musicians.
But did you know Louis Armstrong? Did you ever know him?

I knew him personally. He was my friend. Well when he was at the play down here, I was listening to him and he says, I'd like to dedicate this next number to my little fat friend, Johnny Gidroyd. I was a little star at that time, you know, and he called me his fat. And then I met him in New York, and we were palsy-weldy, and I loved to hear him play. And when he was on the coast, my brother used to go out to the cotton club and they were friends. And he was one of the finest men I ever met, I mean as far as I know.
But did you know him in New York you say?

Yes, he was playing with Fletcher Henderson, a band that played strictly arrangements. Lewis was lost in that band. That's why I said, Fletcher, won't you let Lewis do, it don't mean a thing if you ain't got that swing and Lewis, you know. And Lewis did it. The place woke up, they came alive.
What year was that? Do you remember?
I left a look in this scrapbook. It's in here.
Well when did you make your records? Was it near the time you made your records? Yes. Well I can look that up you see.
I was making the records in those days.
Well we have books that tell all about your records.

You see if I had been like, I was doing so well and I was so busy that I didn't have time to put dates on anything or who the person was. I played in the All-Star Orchestra in Chicago when I was at the Green Mill. I played at the Green Mill in Chicago for Tom Chimali. And I was this trumpet player selected to play with all the stars and I can't tell you who they were and I know they must be all famous musicians. I went there to some big ballroom, we sat down, they handed out the music, we played it. The piano player gave us all a check and right now I don't remember one musician. And there was an array of stars. Did you record this? No we didn't record this. We gave a benefit performance. There were great benefits. You see in New York City they used to put my name on every program, whether I showed up or not, because I was a transferred member. I was only allowed to play in one place until six months had expired. You know the transfer member. And I played at the six day bicycle races with my band for the poor children's tours and I didn't ask the union and they find us ten dollars a piece. But everybody played for nothing but I said you should at least ask us could you play. I didn't think it was necessary. And when they announced my band you'd be surprised how many people from New Orleans were in this bicycle race, prize fighters, prize fighters, trainers, bums, and come up to see me. You know what I mean? And we played about four tunes and this is the truth. There were a lot of, Vincent Lopez, Paul Ash, all big shots sitting in a box, they'd offer a hundred dollars for a sprit to get the bicycle riders to race one another. Otherwise they'd just go around and around and say, Vincent Lopez offers a hundred dollars for a sprit. Vroom, they struck me. The next morning my phone ran incestually. Every agent wanted to book my band. And the only one I wanted to talk to was Vincent Lopez because I know him. You see? So I was under contract. The union allowed me to stay there for six months and then I'd have to join the union. And about that time I got enough of a union. I should have stayed there. I had everything in my home. I came home and people were glad to see me again. And I continued. But it's bad to play in one place too long. No matter how good you are they know what you're going to play before you play. They know how you play it, they can sing it. The only thing I loved about it was that I played, I had a job at Cowbs in the winter and I could go to the White House in the summer. They gave me a share of stock in the golf club. I didn't have to pay any green fees. I could go fishing. What did they set for? And I played three hours at night, no Sundays. Don't get it. Now, why don't you want to know?

Okay. How would you contrast the public taste in music, especially in New Orleans, as it changed during the years from the first that you remember to about 1930? What kind of music did people seem to want in those years, at various times?

Well, for a little while I was not a leader. I had been leading the orchestra for St. Charles. It was a dramatic stock company. Two matinees a week. Oh, it was a darling job. And I decided I would take a rest to get my lip a rest. So the only time I'd know what was going on was when I'd go out and they were all playing the same, playing the same music. It's just different tunes. They all play with a beat. And all of them did free radio programs for publicity, including yours truly. And well, it's just hard for me to tell you, but I know that when I went, I was playing at the St. Charles and it was so warm and they had a typhoon fan or something, there'd be more noise than the people on the stage. They closed. But I had them hooked for a two year contract. So they asked me if I would go into the signing I was putting on the public shows, and they gave me more money. They raised my pay. And I was the feature trumpet player and assistant band leader. If the band leader, if the master of ceremonies got sick, I'd take over the show, you know, which I did, direct the show. So it's just like being locked up. You only play their music, you see? And I wouldn't take anything. I was trying to stay in the business. I didn't want to play too much. So I took the job as second trumpet, and featured man on the stage. But in the pit, when we played, Mr. Capira played the first trumpet, an excellent trumpet player, so I had no responsibility except to memorize the show. And so I couldn't tell you what was going on all the while I played at the Sanger. But when I came out of there, I went out to Suburban Guns with the big band. I went back in the show business. And at that time the Club Forest was bringing named bands, all the big bands, and they had the gambling, and all we had was slot machines. We had big stars but we didn't do the business. So they had to get a cheaper band. So then I decided to do strictly commercial, you know, spot jobs we used to call them spot jobs. Here there are conventions and all like that. And subsequently I built it up fine. I was a house band at the Edgewater in Biloxi. I got every convention they ever had over there. And the convention manager at the Roosevelt gave me everything. He could recommend it because I knew how to play. When I played for people who were past 40, I played two beat music.
What years were that, that you're talking about?
Well I guess that was in the early 40s.

How about back in the 20s, did you notice a great difference between the music that the young people wanted, the style that they wanted, as opposed to the more middle aged people that catered to different tastes?

I'll tell you the truth. With a Dixieland band such as mine, we didn't worry about what they wanted. We played what we wanted. We were a Dixieland band, see? But when I went into the Forest Grill, I started getting the young college people, and I catered to them, so I would mix in a slow tune now and then. But they danced everything, you know? And I would say that the middle aged people went and moved for Tubi. Because when I used to play the alumni dances, then I had to load a band down.
But I wouldn't play them with a Dixieland band.

I'd play them with a big band, see? Because although you weren't getting the money, you had a song like Glenn Miller, you know, all the rest of them, you know. But I don't see much difference in the style of dancing, except young people, they don't dance.
Not now.

No. They don't dance. And as far as rock and roll, I never did look at it, you know what I mean? The only concession I ever made was I let the rhythm play, because it didn't seem to have the, what I wanted, that circle, you know? So I wouldn't offer an opinion as an expert as a style of dancing, but I don't know, I got along fine with it.
What dances do you remember the people doing specific, like foxtrots, tangos?

Oh, they used to, it's according to who's giving the dance. If it's a company dance or a convention dance, you know. I even played polkas. Because during the carnival season we used to put on a couple of carnival balls away from the auditorium by tourist bureaus, and they'd bring people who liked to dance the music, perhaps that we were not used to playing. But being commercial, and I was commercial, I had everything in the box. I even had Yiddish music, I even had music in five-four time for Greeks, if they wanted to. Most musicians can't play five-four time, but I mean, I could, it's pretty hard. But I was lucky enough to have good instruction. And then when I played for Tom Chamale, he was a Greek, and we'd get to start spot, you know, you know there's a Greek wedding, something like that, we played five-four music. But I didn't play for Tom Chamale as a leader. I was important. He brought me up, he came down here to hear me. I played with a band called Arnold Johnson's Orchestra. And they were under the direction of Paul Weichmann. We toured Ohio, and we toured Pennsylvania. I got tremendous money too. I was the feature trumpet player. And we had a whole season at St. John's Casino and Carl Gables. But, uh, I did.

Do you think that the orchestras are like, we're trying to talk mostly about what I was mostly concerned about was up until about 1930, if you can kind of keep that in mind. Yeah. Do you think that orchestras like Vincent Lopez, Paul Weichmann, Leo Reismann, and so forth, had much influence on what people wanted to hear here in New Orleans? I think so.
I think so.
What kind of an influence do you think it had? A bigger sound? Was that being part of it?
It was the big band song.
Dixieland musicians.

Dixieland, understand I never did stop playing Dixieland, but didn't call it that. Because when we finished the arrangement, we finished it in big band style. But when we got down to one of the special choruses, you could meet the five men that get up and give them a-
Just like Whiteman did sometimes. Yes, he did, he did. Like Mississippi Mud. Yeah.
Well, we'd have a number that, it was up in tempo, could be played Dixieland, and then my Dixieland group would get up. And then we'd modulate right back into the last chorus and go out to see it.
When did you first hear the term big band, or when did you first start using that? Was that-
Well, I only started using it, when did I start using it? I started using it recently, you know. They were all big bands. They were all big bands.
What years would you say that they started with a real distinctive big band style? Would it be about like the late twenties, or somewhere in there?

I would say the middle twenties. Middle twenties? Yes, yes. Duke Ellington and such, you know, and Ray Miller. You see, as I told you, I signed up with Vincent Lopez's office. Not that I needed a job, because I was working. But it's good to have somebody looking out for your interest, you know.
Yeah.

So they sent us over to the Arcadia Ballroom and they had Ray Miller there, and he had Frank Trombauer, I guess if you heard of him, played a C melody saxophone. Mike, how you played it. He had the greatest musicians in that band. Well that was the featured band. So this fellow, Fagan, who ran the place, he wanted to hear us and we played. He says, boy I'd like to put you and this band on the baseball field and see who can play the loudest. We played as loud as this big band. But Dixon, man, we hit it. You know, I mean, we didn't lay back. If we took a soft course it was just part of the arrangement. And strange as it may seem, although we played without music, we played arrangements. In the head. I mean we tried to keep the good stuff. We couldn't remember that. No Dixon man remembers what he played yesterday. You know what I mean? It's always new and it comes out of your head. You know, you might find the licks reminiscent, but it's hard to, like when you say, write it down. You write it down and you play it, it sounds terrible. You know, it doesn't sound, it must be spontaneous. So Fagan says, you fellas are great. He says, when can you start? I said, I can't start. He says, well where did you come here from? I said, my agent sent me.
He said, I'm working.

He went on at a rate. And he told the agent, don't send any band here, they can't take the job. And the man said, thought he had a prize. And he did. Because we filled that, there was two isle codes, you know, one would open and a big band and they'd open up and you know, it was done in an artistic style, but it was strictly a ballroom. And you know, it isn't like this. Because truthfully, I don't think there was anything there that played like us. Now the Memphis Five were very popular and they played very well. And the Wolverines were popular and played well. But they didn't play in New Orleans. You see what I mean?
They didn't play. They played true Dixieland.

Oh I see. They played with a beat and they had good men. I remember distinctly that one Sunday, we gave a Sunday matinee, and I had to play the matinee for which I got off on Monday night. The other band called themselves the Circle Quintet, and they were my friends supposedly, but I think they would like to take me down a notch or two, you see? So they brought Bix Spider back in there. Well I said, is that Bix Spider back? They said yes. I said, well I have nothing to worry about. And I went home. Because it wasn't Bix's fault. It was the accompaniment he was getting from that other band who knew nothing about Bix Spider back. But his own band was a star. And they used to make records very good. But it wasn't Dixie. Mm-hm. But it wasn't Dixie. Mm-hm. I was selling Dixie Land band. And when I played the first tune in the Balcanese the people went wild. in the Balkan Age, the people went wild. And you know what it was? Red Hot, mommy remember that? It had a beat. They said, that's the Balkan Age, and we packed that joint, and I had my name in the lights, and I never even took a picture of it. I didn't worry about it. I don't know what kind of a…
Where was the Balkan Age?
At 66th and Columbus. It's a continuation of Broadway. You know what Columbus cycle?
Well, I'm not familiar with it.

They had four places in that one building. Ours was the ballroom. We had Healy's Restaurant on the bottom floor. About that time, the Duke of Wales was cutting quite a sloth in New York. He was a ladies' man, and he used to go to Healy's, and maybe he helped us, I don't know. But it was a very popular spot, 66th and Columbus.

Talking about style, on your other interview you mentioned arguing with the Captain Strykfuss about the kind of music you'd play on the boat. He said something about he wanted you to play like what he'd heard in St. Louis, and he says you're in New Orleans and you play like what people in New Orleans wanted. How would you contrast the two? What would be the…

I didn't contrast them because I didn't know what they played in St. Louis. But to give me a list of ten best tunes in St. Louis that some of them I'd never heard of, but didn't know how they played out. I just said, Captain, I play New Orleans music. And I don't think that the people in New Orleans want to sing most music. I said, I don't know what it is. And then he said to me, he said, well you're working against me. I said, Captain, I'm not working against you. I said, with all due respect to you, you're a fine man, but you're never going to be bothered with me again because I'm never going to play on this boat again. Well what year was that? Oh, I retired in the 50s. Now I would say it was in the 50s. I see. I see. And he said to me, you play good, honest music. I said, I know what you have to do. I wouldn't give him a thing because he was a Martin man. You see when he pulled out from the wharf and you were in prison, he misbehaved and put you in a brig. And he wanted to be everything. I said, Captain, why don't you let me run the boat? You run the band and we'll both wind up on the wharf. Well I'll tell you what to play and how to play. But the trouble was it was the other musicians. They say, Johnny Dwight only plays for you in Lent. They said to me, you want to play for me in Lent? I said, Captain, I play for you and I can play for you. Do you want me in Lent? If you don't, I'll go play somewhere else. He couldn't understand that. Because he had people who played well but were not like Dutch Andrews, who I think is a fine trumpet player. Dutch can't read. I tried to use him and he couldn't read. But he has a big tone and he plays nice and if he'd only had sense enough to make some of the other fellas play a little soft and let Dutch do a little playing, you'd really hear something because his licks clean, he plays nice. That's it. They would, he would take advice from people who didn't know anything about music. See? And then he's always fun with the microphone. And I'd go up and get a cup of coffee. I know what I'm going to do and I'd give to Dom B and I know how my band's going to play or else they're going to hear from me. You know what I mean? And I'm not going to change my style of playing on the boat doing like, I'm playing for the country club, I'm going to play for the same of them. Because I got the engagements because I played the style that they liked. See? And I must have had something. People don't put out a lot of music, pay over. I made it. I shouldn't say that I made it. I was $500 a night just for myself. If somebody likes you and they had the money, charge them. That's all. That's $500 for you? For me, yeah. Not the band? No, no. I used to, Mr. Cobb used to let me off when I'd go up to Greenwood and play for the society people. Give you all kinds of money. Greenwood, Mississippi? Yeah, and the Delta. Other places. You
ever been there? And you're always playing Dixieland

for those things. Played Dixieland? We'd take a tune on Vula Boo. You never heard of that, did you? Well they had nice changes. What does it go? Bo La Bo? Bo La Bo. Oh yeah. You've heard that. We'd make 50 tunes on that thing. And then we used to do a lot of gymnastics. You know trombone plays, you used to put the slide down on the floor and he'd move his head instead of moving the slide. And we'd strike poses, that didn't mean a thing. But that's what we're doing, you know? Yeah, sure. And being young guys, we'd dress, we wore silk suits with big six dollar black leather ties and they looked like a million bucks. Well they were making money, you know. You have to know what to do. I think it's 50% of what you're doing, 50% of what you know, you know? And then you've got to be kind, you've got to be polite, you can't be telling people off, you know? Unless you want to tear up with them like I'd

go on forever. Were you conscious that the people here through the years had a different musical taste than in other parts of the country, that you were playing something really quite different than what people would be listening to say in Chicago or Los Angeles?
Well in the Balkan age we play strictly Dixieland, you know. But we play popular tunes in Dixieland style. Sure. Sure. And the fact that we packed the place, they must have liked it.
Something different, something new, pretty much of them. Well of course I was different.

And I made my point to be entirely different than the other band. See? But fortunately for me the other band couldn't play like we played. I mean they may have had it but they had never done it. In fact they were fine fellas. Some of them came down here to the normal street shows and I'd go over and see them, you know. In fact when my pianist got sick in Harrisburg, he operated on for appendix, I used to bring a man from New York. You know, I went up there, I bet they had a dance hall hall hall. And they wanted something outstanding. So Vincent Lopez sent me and I was coming home. That was the week I was supposed to come to New Orleans. So we finished. The last note we played was in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania. Beautiful ballroom. And we did make some money. And there were musicians, they were good musicians, but they had their way of playing. We had our way of playing. I'd play a tune and he'd say to me, the other leaders said, that's an old tune. And I'd say yes, but it's not an old tune. The tunes are the old good, you know, if they're good. And if they do something for your band, play them. And I always made a policy. If a guy liked the tune, I'll feed you tomorrow. If you liked it, he'd play the day. That's all. . . . .
Okay, second reel of Johnny Deidreault. We got it going now.
Now what are we going to talk about?
Well, when did you notice when they moved away from using the violins so much in dance orchestras and they just got more towards brass and reeds? What do you think counted for that?

Well I think the thing, the violins didn't fit with two beat music. They could play it, but I mean it didn't fit in that combination and he'd sit there most of the time if he didn't pluck it he'd have it as a rap. You know what I mean? I used the violin to play the shows and I'd let him go. I played carnival balls. I had one violin and fifteen musicians. And when we got through playing false blues I said you can go, Bluett, you can go. And we don't need you because we're going to be hammering our carnival ball, marches and all that stuff. You'd have to have fifteen violins to be heard with three trombones and four trumpets.
You know?

And it's not a symphony. You're playing a ball that tells a story and you try to tell the story with the music. Of course you can't always tell it. Maybe the composer would drop dead if you heard how it was played, but it has to be played according to the ball.
Wasn't it so that the union for several years was requesting that you had

at least one ball? I'm going to tell you about that. The union, but that was early. That was early. Let's see. About 1916 or 1917 they had a rule that you must have one string with every five men. So I took up the fiddle. And my father played the trumpet and I played the fiddle. Now you know you can't hire me. No matter who you are, you couldn't hear that fiddle, but I was getting that five bucks or whatever it was. That was the rule. You had to have so many strings. But the string men did that because they weren't not getting any weight.
Before they had been pretty much the thing in the orchestra for dancing.

Oh yeah, sure, sure, sure, sure, sure. You know some people, they'll just get the habit of saying they don't like brass, but they do. But they just want to be with the crowd that doesn't like brass, and they'd say, they don't like brass. But after a while they got impressed on them that they liked it. When I had the contract at the Jung Hotel I had four saxes, and the social leader, she was a social leader too in town, she tried to bring some social life to the Jung, which it never did have. She says, you have too much brass. I said, what brass? I said, those are not brass. I said, those are reed and stones. She thought they were brass because they looked like brass. They were gold. You don't go and play the saxes. And I was a trumpet player, and if it was too loud, I thought it was my fault. Yeah, I know it wasn't too loud. You know? But they have to have some excuse why they can't bring the business in. At the Jung, a fine hotel, fine people, and I went in, picked them away. But they didn't have the social life. The Roosevelt had it. That's the only way it stood.

I played in the Roosevelt. Did you have a roof at the Jung? Sir? Yeah. Can you take, can you do it? Well, we can just keep on talking. Yeah. Sure you have enough. Mrs. Roosevelt? Uh... You ask me the question, sir. Yeah. Um...

Well, you'd say it was about in the teens, when they went, when they started getting more brass and reeds, and people just sort of, the others just sort of fell away? No, it was when I was going to high school,
and I graduated in 1910. About that time the Union insisted on a string with these five men.
Because of the fact that it was changing over at that time. It was changing over at that time. And

a case in point, I played it. Now, as I explained to you before, when I was going to school I wasn't waiting to study. You know what I'm saying? Mm-hmm. We had a dance job. My father had a dance job. My father was a band leader and a contract. And it was out of what we called a tin roof. There's a lot of difference between people as to what was the original tin roof. But I say it was on Washington Avenue. It was used for a prize fight arena. And they pushed the ring back and the band said, in the ring. And it was so big and had no acoustics. And I was the fiddler. But we happened to come off of a parade job. I don't know what it was. And I had my trumpet, but my fiddle. And the music was flat. So I took the bull by the horns and got my horn out and I played. And we didn't have any string but I had to fiddle in case somebody would. And then the people were satisfied with the music because I had more style and my father was strictly legit. He had a powerful lip and played well. But he couldn't interpolate an extra note. He wouldn't know. You see? So that's how I remember distinctly about the one string. On the old Robichaux arrangements, many of it are here. Well, he played left by the... He was a left-handed violinist, you know.

Yeah. Yes. Yeah. But what I was getting at on that was that a lot of those arrangements that are from his collection that he left have a lot of string parts written now, is it that he would have just discarded these and not used this part as time went on when people didn't want so many strings. Like, for instance, they have cello parts and viola parts and so forth. What kind of orchestras would have used

all those parts? Would have been in the theaters and so forth? Mr. Robichaux was a very fine musician and a very fine gentleman. And he liked me. I mean we got along great. He was the one that I borrowed the orchestration of the panel often. And I concocted my own arrangement of it, you see. And you'd just have to take the parts. The truth of the matter is, in the Dixieland we didn't write parts. We wrote a lead sheet. Which is? With the chords for the piano playing. I'd have to find me doing better than you, you see. And then we'd run over the tune, and maybe we wouldn't. But everybody knew Panama. From hearing it, I don't know where. So Parenti would make his chorus and it would be great, and Barry would play his and it would be great. I'd play one, the other player might take one, and we'd play another song. Or we might play up until the 24th ball and we'd come in on the last eight balls, you know, and sock it out. But the violins went out of mine. They didn't go out, but they weren't used much for dance music. Dixieland and our noisy music was taken over, you see.

So you used to alter the, well, you talked in one, in your other interview about sometimes some new tune came out, you'd get the stock arrangement and then you'd have a few iterations on it and then you'd

have your own. Well I'll tell you what, the stocks used to come out so fast that I couldn't make arrangements on everything, you see. So I would trick it, what I call it trick it, trick it up. And it got so that when the other band leaders would come on the boat, just to hear what I was doing, they'd say, playing all specials. I'd say yes. That was the stock. I'd let the saxophone play, get them to play eight bars of Blue Moon, you know, and then when the other guys come in, it sounds like quite loud, it sounds like a big band, you know. Or I might start changing the introduction. Some introductions some bands couldn't play. I'll give you one. One example, there's an arrangement called the Sugar Bowl Medley now that consists of Way Down Yonder in New Orleans and The Saints. It's published. And the introduction goes, half the saxophone players can't get the notes out. If it was left to me I could give them two half notes on the bar so they could be swinging when they got into the thing. Well we used it in the Shrine Band. I said, let's cut it out. You fellas can't play it. They don't like to hear that, you see. I was the leader of the Shrine Band for 1971 and 72. And I had wonderful plans for them, but they didn't go along with me. They preferred to have a good time with me. Rather than sectional rehearsals. They didn't want sectional rehearsals because you'd find out who was making the bad news. They couldn't fool me. I could tell them from where I was standing. You know? But they're all men and means and they're just not getting paid and they pick up their own walk right now. And they had 35 men one night, nine the next. Sometimes they'd be playing, I'd stop directing and be playing. I'm reached in but they're playing. I can't stand it. I can't go with that kind of stuff. But the improvement under me was so remarkable. Even with that mess. When they found out that I didn't want it anymore. I said the only thing that could bring me back
would be money. I mean it. Well, nothing against it. In this day and age I'm not leaving my wife

at home at night to go play around in blue lodges. I'm a Shrine and all that. Mason is all right, there's a lot of crap too. But I'd rather stay home so my wife is safe. She's by herself and we live in the damn big house and leave a thousand burglaries. So I'm not coming with you. I don't need any money. But if I'm going to put up with that stuff, I go to the convention. I pay my way and then I play music. For what? Nobody else plays. Are they down to dancing? And we damn fools wept. They're playing. And half the time it was the wrong place. I won a prize in Memphis with two alto saxophones, a tuba, a drummer and three trumpets. I wonder how I saw them. My wife said this to me. She ought to know. Two alto saxes, both of them couldn't blow their nose, a drummer and a tuba, they were all right. Mike Chapler played the trumpet. He still plays like he did four years ago. He played the sugar blues. We played the Billboard March, the sugar blues, and we got a big medal, big prize. And a couple of them. How lousy were the other bands. I was like, oh. But the only thing we had was decorum. I said to these guys, I said, now when you go on that bandstand, you know in uniform, you're all standing at you see. Don't sit down until I give you the seat. They all sit up and they're like this, oh, just now what life happened. They sat down, oh, they're just a discipline, you know what I mean? The other guys are going to strike like a baritone dragon and like that, you know, and knock the music stands down. I believe we wanted it on our department. This thing you can cut all that out.

I don't like to talk. I don't have a stick. Sure. I'm curious to know about some of the other orchestras. How would you describe Robichaux and the kind of jobs, what kind of jobs did he get, do you know of, and Perrone? Well, as I told you, I was- You're so busy yourself.

I was so busy that I, but I used to tell Mr. Grimowall and Mr. Cobb that I would like to know what the others are doing. So I'd like a night off once in a while, you see? So I'd go out and see Perrone, and he knew me, and he was a crippling violinist. He wrote, I wish I could shimmy like my sister Kate, you know, and I don't know whether he got credit for it. And I would listen to the bands and see what they're doing, and perhaps if I didn't think it's good enough I wouldn't shimmy. Because my father always told me when I'd get ready to make a change in the band, he said, son, never break up a winning combination. And I had it proven to me so much. One night I had Al Belanco who is now a leader. He was playing second trumpet with me. He's a nice looking fella. He sang well, especially western tunes. He sang like a cowboy and that's all I used him on. He had what I wanted. I was loaded and I was singing. And he was in the hospital and I got the Marion Sutter, whom I consider, I guess the best dance trumpet playing in the city, for me. He had a beautiful style, always played clean, no fuss. He's now an officer of the union. So I was playing up at Reserve and I was very popular in Reserve. I used to pack the joint up. If we wore blue pants and a white coat or a white coat and a blue pants, when we come back the next time all the kids would have the same uniform. You know what I mean? They admired us though. And so Sutter's playing there and I'm really, oh I'm having a good time now. Let me play first. I split the book. And I'm loving the way he plays. The manager comes up and he says, where's Al? I said Al's in the hospital. I'm looking up, where's Al? That's too bad. Tell Al to help me. I said, but you've got Marion Sutter here. I said, Al's in the hospital. He says his first trumpet was the Dawn Busters. You know what, WWL? They used to have the Dawn Busters. Pinky Vinakovich had a fine orchestra. Al Hurt was the first trumpet. They played about, they played nine hours a week for $94 a week. Yeah. They get up about four o'clock in the morning. So I said, that's Marion Sutter. I said, he's helping me out. I said, Al is, I said, he's the best trumpet man in town. He said, that's what you say, I still like Al. Well, I said, I'm glad of that. He liked Al. I went, Al couldn't open the case. Al was a good all-around man. He sang good western tunes and he was handsome. He made a big hit. I kept him in my band for 13 years. I never made any changes because my daddy used to tell me, don't break a winning combination. And I think that's good advice. And I'd hear another drum roll player. I said, I'd like to hang out there. And I think about what my daddy said. And you know that members of your band have their friends too. So you've got to give them all a chance. And like I told you before, when I found out a guy I liked to tune, I featured him. And he played him. There's a lot of psychology.

I was curious to know if you felt that, actually, you did go around the country and other places. Yes. Did you feel that you were really ahead of the trends coming from New Orleans, that they discovered a lot of things just a lot later and picked them up, things that had been done a long time before here, like when you were a kid or just coming up in music. And that it just took the rest of the country a long time to discover what was going on here. I think that New Orleans music had an

impression on it, because we used to play on radio, you know. I did a program every Sunday on WWL, and I got plenty of fan mail. When was this? Do you remember? Approximately. That was after Suburban Gardens, and the public's house closed in the early 40s. It was in the 40s. I see. Because I worked steady all the time. And one night I came out of the jazz club. I went on the board of the jazz club. I would talk about it because Miss Moe told me that when I counted the ballots, I didn't have one dissenting vote, which is quite a compliment, you know, because I had opposition for a new member of the board. And they liked me so much. And they used to introduce me every Sunday, that there'd be monotonous. One Sunday they introduced me to the audience, and I wasn't there. I was, you know, when I come out, they said, oh, there he is. Give me a big answer. But I, so I was in the men's room, and a man says, you don't know me at all, Johnny. He said, you, the reason why, perhaps the reason why I'm here. He says, when I was a youngster, and you'd come on the air at WWL, he said, I'd get my drums up and I'd play with you. It made me feel good. There's a man, you know, he, radio was far-reaching. I'll tell you why. Because when I was making the trip over to Biloxi, boy you had to wear khaki clothes and leggings and you'd have an average of five flats to get over there. You'd take a boat and then you'd row through the woods, the chef wrote, finished at Chef, and then you had to get a ferry. And I'm in a place getting gasoline, and a little bit of pump, they rolled it out, and then I hear Ray McNamara playing along. He's out there with the squirrels, you know what I mean? So I was, radio, it's everybody. I used to play in pieces, I never thought I existed. Like, you ever hear of Pankerville? Pankerville. Pankerville. Shortbread town. It's the river they have on, Pasooma, isn't it? Somewhere out there in the country. Yeah, I used to get there. They heard me, and I go there, and it's a nice nightclub, you know, nice people. I played in places when I see the outside, I said, they can't be, they can't afford this band. I go in and I say, is there a dance here tonight? I say, yeah. Well I'm Johnny E. Drighton, the ball is, Johnny O'Brien. And when the people come in, they're all dressed up, nice people. I play nice. I think, how can they do it? I don't know. I used to play in Natchez, this is the truth. I said, Mr. Junkin, how can you pay this band? We don't have anybody here. He said, John, let me worry about it. He had a gambling joint in the back then, he was taking their money. My saxophone player, Franzella, was great too. He made so many passes, he said, come here John, get the saxophone player, I don't want to play sax, I'll have to take my money. So I said, Franzella, come out of that damn job. He said, well, my woman, I said, you're going to play saxophone and stay out of the game with me. That's all. Because it wasn't so much that Franzella was winning, everybody was betting on Franzella, making passes. So then I found out how, but they were building the roads up there on Natchez. And Mr. Junkin, he owned a lot of gravel pits or something like that. And he put up a crude thing to give them the workers and the entertainment, because there was nothing in that nature, you know. So he brought my band. I said, look at that, and they paid me. I look at the game, nobody coming in. They'd dance, maybe take a drink, but it wasn't a dance. It was where you have a crowd that paid at the door to dance. But he was making it.
But how many members were in your band in the twenties?

In the twenties. Now let me explain to you. I would give them anything they wanted. I had big bands. I'd picture here, show you, oh, old Star outfits. I had seven key men. Two trumpets, three saxes, and three rhythms. And I used to use them. For a while I used Ted Demuth, he's the leader here, isn't he? Ted. Yeah. Yeah. A fine trombone player. And Ted was in the Marines at that time. He used to come on a boat in his Marine uniform to play the first set, because he just so much could make it. And I wasn't going to stop the guy from making dollars, making drills, you know. Ted didn't have it so sweet, you know, in the beginning. I don't know what he was doing now, but he's a darling fellow. He's one of the nicest people I ever, he used to come late so often on his yard. The fellows used to call him the late Mr. Demuth. But he didn't, he was a good guy. He's my friend of the Union now, you know. He played with the Oriental Man the last concert, didn't he? Yeah. See, you know, they said, they do well. I don't know where they carried me back. And did you kill me when you put my pitch up there on the last, the last? Oh, I said, now who did that? I didn't know anything about it, you know.
Do you remember orchestras that were back in those days that sounded like the New Leviathan Orchestra does?

Well, I would say that most of the theater orchestras sounded like it. They weren't as big as that, you know what I mean? No. Because they start putting like Lowestate and the Palace, they put a ton of sax in a pit. Alvin Galladora played alto sax at the office. You read Alvin Galladora? I know him, yeah. He's one of the greatest. You know him? Yeah, sure. He's great. He's great.
Can I see that picture for a second? So that's more of a character? That's uh, Miss Durio,
Durio, she's an operatic singer. She was my vocalist on big jobs. That's more, that, uh, the New Leviathan
arrangement is more of something that's characteristic of the theaters, you'd say, than the dance jobs? No, no, no.
It's characteristic of a stock arrangement with fiddles, you know what I mean? It sounds, it has to, it has to. Where would,
where would one have found that sort of thing mostly back in the, say, the twenties? Where would you find it?

Mostly, yeah. Where would you? Well, you'd find any of the shows that had orchestras big enough to play something, but they also played for the pictures, you know what I mean? Yeah. We used to have to feature the pictures. Yeah. I only had eight men at the Liberty when I was directing the orchestra at the Liberty, and I used to play pop tunes all the time for the Overtures, but I used to, sometimes I'd throw slides and invite the audience to sing. And I had a couple of friends who liked to sing, and I'd take the lunch hour and I'd put the song on, because I wanted to holler and light and yell. I had a guy, a broker, used to leave his office and come over and sing. Where was this at? At the Liberty. It's a parking lot now.
Oh, more progress. Yeah, more progress.
We'd chase pictures every weekend. I had a feature picture every weekend. But they furnished us, we had a beautiful library called Galaxy of Picture Music. And you could get music to fit most any
scene. So the theater's one place you'd hear. Where else did you?

Now, now, I took you off from the theater, which was strictly long here, until I went in there, and when I started playing that Charno We Own A Lot To You, with the mute, the house came down, it became a feature. So the Palace had to do the same thing. And they had better jazz men than we had, and Melvin Berry, who was my trombonist tonight. You see, the boys used to double. Now, Santa Picora, was my, when Berry went to California, Berry got a big job out there. Santo came in my band. Santa Picora, you know him, don't you? I met him. Interviewed him in November. He played with me when he was only seventeen. When we went at the tuxedo, he came with a pink great machine shirt on, but he wants to kill me when I tell that to people. It's the truth. He didn't know that. His father was a tailor, he should have known better. But that band used to dress. Oh boy, I would dress when it was good for me to look good. But Santo was playing an act at the Palace one time and the man said to the leader, he says, you know, the trombone play, he's not playing my music. And the leader said, I think it was Fulco at the time, he says, you know, he's a great jazz man, and he never makes, the guy said, don't apologize for him. He says, he plays it better than my music. You know? So jazz took a hold of the orphanage to such an extent that I used to have to stand up in the pit and bow with the axe. They actually asked me to get up from the stage, because my interpolations
helped their music. Were they calling it jazz at that time?

Exactly. My first band was called a Jazz Sass band. They didn't call it jazz, it was called Jazz Sass. J-A-S-S, if you want to look through here you'll find it, S-A-S-S. And we called it jazz. Mr. Grunwald called it the Jazz Sass band. And that was the name it was called, Jazz Sass.
It sounds funny, but that's it. How about ragtime music? Do you remember

it? Oh, I played plenty of ragtime music. At the same time you're playing? I'll tell you what we used to do. We'd play a dance. Like I tell you, there was a place called the Oddfellas Hall. They had a hard one. And we'd play numbers like the eccentric rag or Empire Rag or something like that. And we'd get up with the trumpets and we'd play it over the railing. All the way to make a lot of notes, like Down Home Rag. Remember the Down Home Rag? Yeah. That was a good number to show off to trumpet guys, doesn't it? We'd have three trumpets, two altos, pick-horns, a baritone tuba, and two drums. One guy played a bass drum. And we made good bands. We played shottishes, we played lances, we played varieties. You ever hear of those?
I haven't heard of varieties. I've heard of the other ones. You heard of lances? Oh yes.

We'd make a roll and now we'll have a lances. They formed their groups. You know how they do it. They go in and out. It's more like the square dancing and round dancing that you see today, see? And the fact that we'd stand up and play, it was a little different. My father used to give the trombone play a dollar extra every time we played tromboneum. There's a number called tromboneum. You know we didn't make a lot of money in those days. The scale was fine. Some guys would cheat and play for fours.
You played carnival balls back in the twenties a lot?
I want to present you a little bit. Oh, thank you.
Were you playing carnival balls a lot back in the twenties?
No. I wasn't available.
You were too busy with your other work.

Yeah, but in the forties, I was the fifties. I was the official man for Rex for about twenty years. I played in the old carnival. I had thirty-five. I could make a living in the carnival season. Because you play a suburb dance, you know?

Do you think that had a lot to do with the fact that they had the carnival here? Do you think that has a lot to do with the fact that you had so much music in New Orleans because you had a big call for

the dance bands? During the carnival season, we sometimes had to engage men from the symphony, if they were available. There's always a shortage of men during the carnival season. Yes. And then some of them like big orchestras, you know, and some don't. But they like to make a splash, you know, or the captain does anyhow. And if you can talk, you've got a good line. For instance, if it was too light a ball and I had solos, like I told you, if we had played balls, bluett or something like that, I'd get Albert Curse, who was one of our fine, and I'd let him play the rock in the microphone when he got through and say, Al, you can go because they're not going to hear you. You know? The strings didn't count too much. French horns and trumpets, yeah, they got a chance, and the trombones. We used on average four trumpets and three trombones. The four trumpets, you see, they would spell one out because the grand march would last a long time.
You know how I used to- What years was this now, you're talking about all these four trumpets and three trombones?

Oh, in the forties, in the forties, up to fifty-nine. We used as many men as we could. We tried to engage those men for the whole season. So you'd be sure you have them. You'd give them all the dates, and I'd make them sign it, but they accepted the dates. See? Then you have, by the time after you play one or two balls, you've got an organized orchestra, because they're good musicians. And they save you a lot of trouble. You don't do a lot of talking. They know what you're going to do, you know what I mean? And that's a great thing. But case in point, I never would take a steady job after I left the setting, you see. And the Broadwater Hotel used to hire good orchestras over in Biloxi. And the manager asked me to play with it, and I couldn't. I didn't want to. So one time he said, Johnny, my band's one day late, I don't have a band. And he sent me a band, and I sent him a pickup band from the union. So next time I went there myself. And he says, I want to tell you something. He says, you know that band you sent over here? He says, I just had to tell them. He says, I went up and told them, you fellas have never played a job in your life together. That was the truth. He says, every time you play a set you have a union meeting. What are you going to play? He says, Johnny comes here, he says his manager puts the lights on, puts the music racks, he walks out on the band's tent and says how to do folks and starts. And he says, I have a little word. I call out the numbers. There's no discussion, let's play this and let's play that. An organized band doesn't play like that. You don't have that in there. You build your sets. You start, you play to a climax if you're going to play. You want to finish. And when I'd say, that's all, that was my, when I'd say that's all, in fact they used to pick it up in the newspaper, they said, you'll have a good time until Johnny says that's all. You know what I did a little? I'd show you some write-ups from here that said, with the exception of my trumpet playing, there was nothing in the show at the off, he was married. But that's how the guy wrote up the show. With the exception of Johnny's trumpet playing, there's nothing of merit in the show. And there's eight acts including Jack Benny and all of them. The guy must have loved me. I wasn't lucky.
What do you remember about singers singing to the megaphone? Do you remember much about that period?
Yes, yes, who used that? Sure. Who used to sing for you? Well, in Biloxi, George Potter, my banjo player,
was my son. And he sang to a megaphone. When did that go out? When did you start using microphones?

When I went out with the microphones. I was the first band leader in town to own an amplifying set. Amplifying set? Yeah. When would that be? I used to carry it around with two speakers. I mean, what year was that? Oh, I went through here. You see, I used to play a lot of cardboard balls in Mobile. And they write me a lot of fank. I mean, that's how I get the dates, because I don't remember dates. And I remember that I used it over there first. It was called
the quarter box. You want me to look through it and find Mobile for you? Well, I can do it. It'll help you.
I used to play a lot of people. I used to play the Hattiesburg Country Club. I used to play the Hattiesburg Country Club.

Oh, that was a not-willing job. I stayed in Admiral Simms for one of my honeymoons. You did? Was Frank Lane the manager? You did what? You think you did, anyway. I think I spent the night there. My honeymoon night, I spent that.

Sule College. Look at the president of Sule College. You see, this was in a fire. I had two washrooms windows when I lived on Cadiz Street, and we used one for the library, and the fire had to break out our face.
Well, when did your- did you use a megaphone right from the first with your band, or when did that start?

Well, I first heard singing. When I had the Dixieland band, we didn't sing. But when I'd go to Biloxi, I'd bring ten men, see? Well, I'd bring ten men, and we'd play a few, you know, we had a big crystal ball, we'd put the lights out, that's all the entertainment we had. That's all the set you had. That's all we had. We didn't have any intermission. He didn't want any intermission, so instead of playing four hours, we played three. We didn't want any intermission. And we sent a couple of cases to post the dance down. And we were glad to get, you know, the one on the west. Sure. You see, because the New Orleans people used to go to Biloxi on the weekend, and they'd get out and everything. It wasn't the local people. Oh, I see. I found it out, because I went over there one week too soon, and I gave an answer, and I charged two and a half, and only had thirteen people. And a friend of mine said, Johnny, there's nobody in Biloxi. He's got two and a half dollars and a half. He said, because there's the local, the New Orleans people that support the thing. People from up in Birmingham, they come down, and people from New Orleans go over to the Gulf Coast. It was a different thing than it is now. So I gave another dance from that choice fifty cents, and I sold thirteen hundred tickets. I thought the fact there was Johnny D. Dwight in the recording orchestra, I could get, you know, make a lot of money. And this was a... Thirteen people. I said, what's... He said, Johnny, they don't have two and a half. So I got the sign, I changed it, two and a half to fifty cents. I made a hundred and ten dollars on the hats. Just on a hat check? Hats. Everybody wore hats and everything. This was what, about mid-twenties this was happening? I can tell you. It takes too much time. If I had known just what you wanted, I'd have to...
So you had a ten piece orchestra that you were calling your recording orchestra, besides your...

The New Orleans country club?

Earl Long. Mrs. Long was a very fine woman and she liked me because of my conduct and so and so. Although they say that Earl didn't drink, he looked to me like he was loaded on something. If we'd have lived here, we had it anyway. All the time I was. All the time? And before I went into the Spartan game, I had to break into a bunch of established bands when I started playing sorority and fraternity dances. And they wanted an attraction. And I didn't want to lose the job because the job is a job. And I'm talking about the things that are tough. And I was a leader, getting a leader. And he liked a lot of vibrato. And he liked too much vibrato. And I played with vibrato, you've got to do it to have feeling. You know that. You're a tromboneist, you use it yourself, don't you? Yeah, sure. Sure. But because I was the contractor, it's you, you know, if you say I think, I just tell him to shut up, when are we going to play golf tomorrow, or something like that. I didn't take any orders from him. He didn't have any music. He came down here with a coat on and a talisman. I put him on his, well that's all right, he's rich and I went to pictures, you know, he's a movie actor. He made a hit, he got punched in the joint, he went through a case, it was on the scene, and he did it so well that he got a lot of attention. He could play, you're the tea, you're the something, my coffee, what's that? You're the cream in my coffee. I never heard a man make so much out of that. He used to play it all out of that. Well, you mentioned the mutes. When did mutes become, what kind of mutes were really popular? Straight mutes. Straight mutes?

Yeah. There was a, Mr. Peterson who was the dean of all the drummers, he taught all the drummers, his name was George Peterson, he used to make them out of fiber. Out of what? Fiber, some kind of fiber. Red. Fiber? Oh, I call it fiber. It's a stiff material. It's a cardboard. And I invented a lot of mutes but I failed to have them copyrighted. But the Dixie Music Company in Chicago had them copyrighted. I invented the cup mute. I used to have a large Salisbury can attached to a straight mute. And when I played it, it was a cup mute.
A Salisbury can?
A large Salisbury cigarette can. It was large, I say large Salisbury because that was the one I used. There might have been other.
How did you get the idea? Just having it occur to you?
I used to play through the big end of a megaphone, through the small end of a megaphone, through a tin can with a rubber plunger, anything for weird effects. A different effect.
And what year would that have been that you?

I did that when, well that's when I started with my success, in 1917. 1917, you got the cup mute then. I took a large Salisbury can and I got some kind of something, put a hole in it, clamped it onto the straight mute and I fixed it in the right direction so I could get a little tone and all of a sudden I had a nice tone, had a nice cup mute. So it was. If I had to have that copyright, I'd have been rich because they came out in different sizes and different levels.
You wouldn't have had to play all these years.

You'd just sit back. I'll tell you, I neglected so much but I had things so easy. My uncle, now this is aside from this, he owned a row, two rows of houses up on the river, commercial living. There was 18 Negro houses in each row. He offered it to me for nothing because he was getting tired, he was very wealthy and I refused. I didn't have time. I didn't have any sense. But I couldn't picture going around collecting for 36 Negro attendance, you know, they got about $9 a month out of the place. And I had some property of my own and I was, I don't know, I might have been big headed or something, I don't know, when I look back, the things that I neglected, I must have been happy playing music or doing something. But I was just having to try to get as much sleep as I could. I was tired all the time. I'd play a carnival ball like you know with fire but not going to have rehearsal at night at Cloud of Gale. The musicians come in, you dare not say a word to them, they're tired, they're just finished, they're tired too. So we'd go through the motions of making the rehearsal, you know. But by the time the ball came on we were fresh. But sometimes you'd have three or four rehearsals, I'd have three or four books going at the same time. And I'd put the music in myself, I had to make the cuts, you know, time it and all. I'll tell you I'm in my money. I wouldn't do that for love of money. I swear I wouldn't.
It doesn't look like it's hurt you anymore.

I'd rather be a side man. Sure. And then you don't have to put up with the captain. And then there's women. And then when I do, I get brainstormed. I had a doctor, he says a letter to my sweetheart. I said that sounds nice. And you know what it was? His whole life. I had to put music to when he was in the army and when he got out of the army, when he recorded his wife, when the first baby was born, all that. He said, you need a score for that. You need an arranger to sit down and time all that stuff. You know? Yeah. And I had a plate, Louisiana, the French flag and the American flag goes up. Yeah. The United States purchased it. So they lowered the French flag or whoever it was, the French flag, and put the American flag on it. What was this so? At a corner of a ball. I see. So I had to play something muted and had the French sport sound sad and the Stars Spangled Banner, you know? It sounds good even if I did do it. I don't think anybody notices but me.
Oh. Well I guess something else. Did you have any, you sometimes took stocks and tricked them up. Yeah. Did you have any favorite stock, people that did the stock composing, arranging rather?
Yeah, Frank Skinner. Frank Skinner was my favorite.
Frank Skinner.
When was he functioning? He functioned a lot, the time that I, in the forties. In the forties.

He was very good. He was very good. He was very good.

Did you have any favorite popular composers, let's say when you started out, say in the twenties, people that were, stick out in their minds?

He wasn't my very best. Gershwin? Gershwin, yeah. I used to love to play that. You know, I've been out since 59, and there's this think tank going back on me, you know. Not too badly. Yeah. Of course, yeah, we're getting a little later. That's in the 30s. I was curious as to whether they were conscious of the fact that they had a lot of people from here who'd gone out and written, you know, music. They thought they were talking about New Orleans music.

This place for a while was a very lively place as far as music was. And composers, song pluggers, they all had agents here. You know? I didn't even know you. $12 cover charge?
Well, $12 minimum charge.
That was a long time ago, too.
Oh yeah.
