I wasn't there enough to him to hear it, because I was not. They asked me, but now you've heard of the Brunese brothers, Merrick Brunus, Abby Brunus, you know one of them died.
Yeah.

And Henning died early in life. He was a great trombonist. And Merrick played a trombone, Abby was a fine trombone, very good one. But he didn't have solidity. You know what I mean? He played in the races and he finally did union moves. But he's a swell guy. He got me up, he pulled me up on a stand on the block in front of a lot of people and he gave me my life's history and all that, and how it made you play. And I said, folks I'm so glad you remember me, you make my fault. I said, but you know me as a pretty fair trumpet. I said, let's leave it that way. I couldn't play, I had no whip. I'm going to get up there and they sang, I thought he was good.
Destroy your reputation.

Man, when I used to play the trumpet, I played for keeps. You know what he used to say about me? He said, you play a trumpet that says, listen to me. I mean, I played and I gave it all, you know? I meant it, I meant it when I played. I don't know whether I was good or not.
Well you must have had emotionalism in your playing, not just a mechanical.

No, no it was never mechanical. I made a record of the two-wing swing that I'm ashamed of now, but I made ten thousand dollars on it so I don't see I should be ashamed of it. And the chorus that I wrote with all those notes in it, I must have got five hundred applications from trumpet players all over the United States. Please send me your chorus of the two-lane swing.
When did the term swing first come in, do you remember?

Well it was, we used to call it the two-lane swing. Two-lane didn't have a song, you know? My band used to fill in with the two-lane band. It was a poor band. My father tried to teach them, but they didn't want, he wanted to teach them for nothing, but they didn't want any discipline. They wouldn't listen to him. My father was a bandmaster in the United States. He saw me. And when he said, if I was a half a mile away and he'd whistle at me, he didn't have to look to see if I was coming. I came. You know what I mean? He was straight. And my father taught to two-lane band free of charge, but he couldn't get anywhere because they cut up too much. So we'd come up with my band from college and we'd play with band. We made a couple of trips. We didn't have any uniforms, we didn't go on the band. Sometimes we'd sit on grass. . .
Yeah, well this is Real Four, Johnny D. Dry. Okay, now what were we saying about swing?
Okay, when was the term swing first to use in your experience?

In my experience, it didn't come in to the big bands and they played those terrific arrangements such as Casaloma Stomp, all this deep Henderson, Tampico, where they had terrific sax choruses. That's what they started to call this band. You see, they had so many good tunes that you didn't have to have a terrific hot band, if you had a big band, that could play even the stocks. And even good bands wouldn't change those stocks. Just like the South Ramport Street Parade, which is recent, but which to me is a classic as far as jazz is concerned. I love it. I have a couple of recordings on it. But in the days of jazz and Dixieland, they didn't refer to swing at all. And to my knowledge, they came in with the big bands. I mean, you know, they'd make new terms, you know.
Do you think that was a new term for something that had been around a long time, really, in terms of the rhythm?
I don't know. You mean the name, the term?
No. Do you think that when they started using that term, that they were just using a new term to describe something that had been around in some form for a long time?
Well, I guess they were trying to describe that it, although it was a big town, a big band, they played with a beat, you know. And they did, because they always had good men, hot men in those bands.
Why do you think they wanted to get bigger and bigger bands as time went on? What do you think that to?

I think because they sound better. You like the big band? Oh, I like the big band. I like a good big band. You know what I mean? If they play a tune, if they're nice arrangements. To me, a barring and sax is something. Isn't that fine? I used to work them to death. I used to put a spell. I used to have a fellow play the tuba with me. He played such fine tuba that he took, in all the introductions, he'd play with the brass. He'd have a note. You know what I mean? I used to like to write introductions. I figured that even if they didn't dance to it, which they didn't, because it took longer than introduction to get on the floor, it sort of was a hero like, like a fan fan. But it was in rhythm, though, you see? And some I would write without rhythm. Just trombone, trumpet, and tuba, and it would sound good, if they played it good.
Well, don't you think they get more of an arrange that's really getting away from the Dixieland a lot further, of course?

Well, of course, you know and I know that the big band had a stay. It did have a stay, and they had good bands, very fine bands. But in spite of the fact that even when I used the big band, I always played Dixieland, you know, because I'd see some people who would never get on the floor unless you played two beats. I know a prominent man, a big man over the river. He'd be sitting at a supper dance and he wouldn't move and he'd be looking at me and I'd say, Johnny, when are you going to play my tune? So I'd say, Hi Society. And then he'd get on the floor. You know Hi Society. And I'd say, Yeah, sure, everybody knows. It's a good dance tune. You have some good jazz clarinet play. And all the jazz clarinet players practically play that same chorus. I don't know who made it, but it was good. You know that little, yeah. That's the variations. Yeah. That's a standard.
How about things like, say, Mr. Jelly Lord. So you remember songs like that? Those old Jelly Roll Morton things?

I'm sorry to say that I had very little knowledge of Jelly Roll. He may have been the greatest. You see, my position is that I was working. And I knew what was around me. And I could only get a night off once in a while, you know, to go hear somebody else play. Did you ever hear A Sweetheart of Mine, that song? No. I know one thing. I believe I was the only orchestra that ever played My Wonderful One, written by Paul Whiteman. I believe that's the only tune he ever wrote, isn't it? I don't know if he really wrote that or not. I don't know. But you know, I made a hit because I could play it. Unless they're playing somebody's country plays, they must have liked it. And they say, You know, only band plays. Well, I said, It's beautiful. But I only played it there. You know what I mean.

I mean, you played these different places, like a phase and so forth. How did people like the dance music divided up? Did they like to have like a couple of fasts and then a slow, or did they like a waltz once in a while, tangos?

Well, you know, as Spanish music got popular. At what time? I said, Well, you know, when I was on a boat, you'd have to play rombas and sambal. They used to have a cargo line sometimes. But not a public player, private player, you know what I mean. They'd never have a cargo line in a public affair or something. But usually, you'd open up with a surefire tune. You'd hit them squint on the face with a tune because if they didn't know it, they might not think, if they think they can't, everybody doesn't know how to dance. So you play it. I know, if I opened up with Stardust, all the kids would be on the floor. They'd love it. See, it's slow. And then I'd take a little jumping chord. You know, and I'd always finish with a lively arrangement. And I played four numbers to a set, usually. Because I'd never, never play a rumba in the middle of a set. I'd open with a rumba because I wouldn't want to. And if the guy didn't want to ask the girl to dance because he couldn't rumba, he didn't have to ask her. But he didn't have to tell her. He didn't have to tell her I can't dance at the same time. A rumba in the middle. You have to use your head. You know what I mean? If I played a tango, open with, if he can't tango, he doesn't ask her to dance. But when you go into high society, you see them all get on the floor. So they must, that's, that's, that's. Because they all know how to dance. Middle-aged people. They could walk around. You know, we used to call them walk around us. Anybody could dance. Anybody could dance. Walk around. You know what I mean? So you have to, I have a fellow come at me, what are you doing? You're a roughneck, you know. What are you doing? See you're playing Blue Room. I said, I wish I was playing Blue Room. Because the music was nice, he didn't like it. It was too sweet and too nice, so I have to go and say, I'm a scat ramble or something for that point. You know what I mean? Taking care of your next piece. I used to have to list them, put down a request.
Do you remember many people Charlestoning? Charleston? Yeah.

I don't know that they Charleston too much on the floor, because during that period, I was playing in the Maiden and the Roosevelt, or the house like that, and it was, people were not, the same club, the same outfit, all strangers like, you know what I mean? But Charleston was very popular. We used to play it. And maybe if we played the country club, we'd do it, and they'd play Charleston, because they knew one another.
Yeah, they thought it was too demonstrative. Charleston was a must, you know, we had to play Charleston. Yeah. Did people dance many other, do the Charleston dance to a lot of different tunes too?

Well, yeah, if you find a tune that you could give them a Charleston beat, you know, you'd play it, and they recognize it. They're smart. Those that dance are smart. You can't say like, the musicians should say the public's stupid. The public's not stupid. Not the people that pay me, they're not stupid. They hired me because they thought they were getting- Because they knew what they were doing. They knew what they were doing. So they're not stupid. But maybe because a guy doesn't know how to dance, but he's enjoying himself. Help him enjoy himself. I played conventions where they couldn't keep time, but they always had a ten spot in their hand. You're going to laugh at that? No. No. No. The musicians, they fall out. But their ideas don't bring in any money. You know what I mean?
You might have good ideas, but they don't pay necessarily.

Well, when anybody would ask for a roll-a-long little dogey, they used to get sick. They'd say, oh no. I'd put it in the metal and get rid of it quickly. You know what I mean? I'd call it something else, and then when I'd finish up with it, because I don't know how many people throw buns at me, you know what I mean? But there wasn't a bad tune.

Did you used to connect the tunes to some of the Society orchestras today? They just, they start a beat up, like Lester Lannan, say, and they just take a whole bunch of tunes, they have it all rehearsed and everything, and they go from one thing to the other with just a little kind of an interlude- Modulation. Modulation, or, and change you out a little bit so that people don't get bored with the same key. Yeah. And then they keep going on for a long time like that. Did you used to play a tune and stop and start another one, or did you keep the same beat a long time?

Well, no. We would play an arrangement on a tune. It was only the hackney tunes. I mean, the tunes that were so well known, we'd play from one to the other. We'd play a medley. And if it was the tune that we didn't care too much about, we'd put it in a medley. See? And we used to play mostly waltz medleys. Unless like, oh, like when you want to sign off, you might want to sign off for the waltz. To Night Sweetheart or something? Yeah, well I had a medley, but the bands used to call Steal It. Down there, it had to change all the time. You know, I used to, you see over in Biloxi they'd be sitting in the chorus and you should see, but when the dancers break out they wanted to give the appearance and walk out the pavilion. You know what I mean? So I had to play a long sign off. So I used to throw them, show me the way to go home. And all the guys, all the people, they were all coming back and, show me the way to go home. You know? I played a couple of choruses and I'd say, good night ladies. And I played just about four balls on the horse field. And I said, that's all, good night folks, glad you came. But everybody knew me. I played for everybody, my friends. We played a morning dance from 11 to 12. It was free for the public. We could get all the young people over. Where was this? Biloxi. The only stipulation was that they had to wear a necktie. So some of them wouldn't have a necktie. They wouldn't let them in the pavilion. So I bought me a dozen, ten cents a necktie. I said, well, wait, put them on my trumpet case. I see a friend of mine, I want him a tie, and he put it on, he'd come in the pavilion.
What years were you at the pavilion about? Was it 32? According to your clippings there, I think it was. 32 to 34. Well, that's not, I think that was the years that you had there.

Well, those were my biggest years when I played in Biloxi, because I was that good at Walter White. I was like, Mr. Cobb used to keep us in the summertime just to have us in the winter. But when he found out that I wanted to go to the White House, he arranged it. In fact, Walter White came there one night with Joe Fulco, and I introduced him to Mr. Cobb. He said, Mr. Cobb, I'm trying to get Johnny every year to come home and play at the White House. He says, it's loyal to you, Mr. Cobb. Well, he says, I keep Johnny in the summertime, I don't make any money. And if Johnny wants to go to the White House, it'll be okay with me, providing he comes back Labor Day. So Walter White said, Mr. Cobb, Labor Day is our biggest day. It's the end of the season. It was the 14-week-end game to see. So Mr. Cobb considered that I should open up the day after Labor Day. So I didn't have to worry. I knew that I was going to play at the White House. I got room and board for my wife and I and my daughter. I got a beautiful room. I got 20% off of laundry. I got $250 a week to play three hours a night. No Sundays. You know that.
Take the play.

My wife and I, my sister's wife, we only had two years, and we made six trips already. We got a couple of them there. We'd travel and go see. And I'd go to shrine conventions, too.

And I said, I'd walk out after the band was set. I mean especially if there was an audience where people were sitting down eating and all, and they were waiting for them. And they got the broad water wonderful place. And the band, and I said, when's the band going to start? Then I walk out, I bow, and I get to the whole beat and they go off. And the band had commotion. And we played requests, but I know what sets to play. And then after 12 o'clock I used to take them into my conference and I said, we're about to open our memory book. Now if you have any tune that you like particularly, and if we can possibly play it, we'd be glad to play it. What would you like us to play? Oh, the request is come on, play our tune. You make the hit with those people that way. You become, you know, they're looking at you all night and they want to talk to you. You know? They think you're a celebrity. You know? I'm just a band leader trying to make a living. You know what I mean? But they like to say, you know who I saw? And they make a big deal. It's something that people are finding. And you meet all kinds of people. I never had any trouble, never, with anybody at a dance because I didn't play right or I didn't play the right music. I had one guy say, I'm all for you for life when I was leaving the jungle. I said, and why? He says, you didn't play night and day. I said, did you ask for night and day? He said, no. I said, do you think I have a crystal ball? I said, I stand up there and read a crystal ball. I said, can't you ask me for it? Oh, he said, that's a must. I said, it's a must only when you ask for it.
It's just one of those nights I didn't play night and day.

You don't know what a band leader goes to. You've got to be smiling when you feel like, you know. But after all, I think I'd do it again. Yeah? Yes, I loved it. And you've got to love music to play. You've got to love music to play in places where the piano is so bad that you turn the back of the piano to the people and tell the piano player, knock the head of note all night, and he sits there and gets his dope, how do you like that? If you ask him to tune the piano and they're $15 or $20, you don't want to spend it. Frank Cuny, my piano player, luckily for me that he could tune the pianos. He carried it. A tuning thing. You know what that big-
Tuning hammer.

Tuning hammer. When we went in, we used to play at what is now Brennan's. That was called the Paddy O'Royle. Remember? Yeah. I was the most popular man with the manager because he knew he was going to get a new piano repair job.
Every time it came around.

The first thing he'd do is say, why are you all drinking? You know what I mean? And Cuny didn't drink. And Cuny used to be the reason why we used to, when we played on the courthouse steps during the Spring Fiesto, I had a big band, Fakin' in the dark, you know. Oh, come the way, it's a trip. You can't forget this, you know. A man said to me, he said, your piano player, he's on the piano more than he's on top of it. I said he's repairing the pedals now, he just got through with the keys. He tuned the piano. He said to me, look Johnny, no choruses tonight, and I'm going to play in the middle register. He'd stay in the middle register. He couldn't go here or there, because it was out of tune. And he wouldn't have time to tune the whole piano. So he'd tune the bad notes and the, you know. He'd be like, I know places. I played in Raceland one day, and that's a terrible place to play. They never tuned a piano ever. I played there and the piano was so bad that the saxes and the trumpets, we didn't have enough slide to pull out. And you play a whole lot of tunes. So I turned the back of the piano to the people. And I said, Frank, don't touch the piano. He said, that's easy. You know? So we played. Azure paid me. He said, good business. We did fine, Johnny. Come back again. I will. Al Streeman goes there. Al Streeman is the guy that sets up the band with white gloves on. He said, you know, he's not queer, but that kind of guy is. He refused to play the piano. The guy says to him, look, we had Johnny D. Droid here last week, and he saw there inside that and knew there was no compassion. He didn't come playing. So Streeman says, what did you do? I said, I didn't use it. He says, I wish. But he's the leader. They expect him to play the piano. Don't you see? He's the leader.
Piano player leader.

You know? He just played the wrong instrument. I did the same thing at the Gulfport Institute over there, college over there, military school. The piano was so bad that the saxophones' mouthpiece were falling. I said, shove him in. Don't play the piano. No one knew that he didn't play the piano all night. So then the portable pianist came out. And Russ Papaya bought himself one. And I was about to buy one. But I decided to quit the pianist to get my voice away. And it canceled. She was so sick. So I quit. And so I quit in 59. I quit. And so I quit in 59. I had calls and calls and calls and wanted me to play, but I said, I don't have any music. I get current in music. I make current to lead the band. I didn't miss it. It's a funny thing to say, how could you retire after all that? You get enough of that too. You get enough of that excitement. I'm going to go. I'm going to tell you the union ought to make the price of carnival balls so high that they wouldn't have any carnival balls. Those people have daydreams up to you. And they want you to put up the music, and you want to give you twelve musicians, and they want you to play Pagliacci all night, you know, and all the big operas. And then when they do the dance, call out, then you've got to be a jack. They don't know. I mean I hire a violin player and I pay them about thirty or forty dollars to play one tune. But remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember to remember Then sometime I'd have to hire him in from the symphony. I had a man play for me, and I play his first trumpet with the Philadelphia Symphony.
I can brag about that.
I said to him, I don't have enough money to pay you, but I want to thank you. He said, Johnny, I can use that $25. Anybody can use me. He says, that's a big kick.
Something different.
Who was his name?

I think his name was Taylor. I saw him in the picture. You see, the New Orleans Symphony is, truthfully, it's composed of people who are coming up or going down. You know what I mean? They don't have the New York Philharmonic or the top notches. But they're good. They come there with the symphony in their pocket. You know, I played in the symphony long enough to know. I played third trumpet in the symphony. And you'd be surprised. Third sounds is nothing. But you get tougher parts than the first guy. You hit the high D sometimes when the other guy's only on his lap. And I didn't know that. And you're not always... If you miss a note, you're finished. Who's going to miss a note? The first symphony I ever played, and I never played it before, of course, I released it, was Tilland's Spiel. You ever play that?
No, I know it, though.
Yeah. It's pranks about Tilland's. Yeah. It opens with the third trumpet. And then the low register. And then the low register.
And then the low register.

Well, I didn't get stage fright, because that would pass. I wasn't used to everything. And the first trumpet was in Chicago. We were in Portland. He said, Johnny, you got something I wish I had. I said, what? That low register. I said, but you got the high one. I wish I had that. He could hit those high notes. He wasn't supposed to hit low notes. He was playing first trumpet, you know? But it was just notes, and fortunately for me it was written in B flat. Most of the trumpet parts were written in D and E flat, you've got to transpose. You know they don't write for the B flat trumpet. You never see that. You get the trumpet, F. You've got to change cleft right away. You've got to know all the clefts. I used to play symphony at five o'clock and go play dance music, and go and play Vauderberg show and then play dance music. But only for the dollar. I was a prostitute, a musical prostitute. You want to ask me some more?
No, I don't have any that I can think of right now.
Are you in a hurry? Well, it's five minutes to five. You have to go.

Well, I'll get her to close the joint up, and we'll make it run until five. They throw me out at five, though. Make me close it up. I want to ask you one question. Well, ask her. Because you were talking and I was out of the room.

Who was Sidney Ayrton? Sidney Ayrton was a sax and clarinet player from Drew Holman. She was a very fine one, very good man. And he played up north somewhere. How I mentioned him, and I have mentioned him a time then, because he wrote Lazy River. You know, Carmichael has his name on lots of tunes, but for instance, when you mention Stardust, you say Carmichael Stardust. But there was a man named Mitchell Parrish who had a lot to do at Stardust, you know. But they don't say Parrish, because, go on, the other fellow is better known, you see.
Yeah.

But you know when I ask any musicians to hum for me the voice of Stardust, they don't know it. I like it. It's pretty good. You know. Yeah. I wrote it for Shockey, but they didn't even tell me thank you. I guess he couldn't play another one.
Yeah. It's interesting. Well, I had a special arrangement on it.
After a while everybody was playing that same thing, so I played it with a public sending on it, you know.
They even steal that.

Well I guess it's a compliment. Well that is a compliment. I know that imitation is a height of flattering. Maybe I unconsciously stole some things too, you know. Anything that's successful is worthwhile listening to. But I've realized that stock arrangements, every band would sound alike if you played the stock.
Sure. It's good for high school and college bands to have that.

Well I mean the first time you play it, because you don't want to rehearse for one tune. I think Peter off at the finish, he would start working in two tunes, you know. We used to say try them on the dog. I don't know why they got that expression or not. They said let's try it on the dog. And I listened to it, and then I'd take it home and I'd cut it up. And lots of times the fellas would say that sounds partly like an old stock I used to do. I said it is partly because if they had a good 16 bars on the finish and I couldn't write any better, I'd paste that 16 bars on my arrangement, you know. Sure. I used to have an arrangement called, Bonnie Rapp gave me, he gave me old truckers, called X-20. It had no title. But it consisted of a lot of good tunes. Avalon, it opened up with whispering with the drum roll. And I lost my heart in Avalon. And it was four tunes, and finished with Strutters Ball. And it was a good rhythm. And it was called X-20. And do you know the people in Biloxi used to come up and go, Johnny would you play X-20? They'd get on to everything. X-20. And I think that they used to dance all the rest of the choruses just to get the Strutters Ball. So why didn't they ask for Strutters Ball? I played more arrangement on Strutters Ball. It was a standard tune, a good tune to fit. And I used to fake after the intermissions, because you know, people are getting drunk. They don't pay too much attention. They used to let each guy play what he liked. I remember when I was talking about blowing bubbles. I had Benny Winnallet playing trumper. He's a fine fellow. He was the greatest drummer playing well. But he was reliable. He was a gentleman. He had a lot of friends. And he didn't give me any trouble. So we all, they're playing a medal in Avalon. Just call it Arton. I had Freddie Newman playing piano with me. You remember Freddie Newman used to be the dormers? He used to play with me at night. I'm good at dawn, I must have sounded asleep at half-time. So Benny says, I'm forever blowing bubbles. And Freddie Newman says, Benny, you better see a doctor. The man broke up. I'll tell you one that's funnier than this. We were playing a fake medley at college one night. And I'd call out the tunes and the piano player, he'd make modulation into the key, and I knew what each man liked. See, but I didn't like to have a lot of discussion like the man said, they have a public meeting on the man's stand. So I called out a tune and they went and I don't know what they did. And I said, for the love of might, do you know what a band went into, for the love of might? You ever hear that, Waltz? That was a Waltz.
No, I don't know that, Waltz. Yeah.

For the love of might. It was a popular moment. It was one of those things like, I knocked the hell out of Kelly. You know, oh no, no. And I said, for the love of might, and my saxes went into the love of might. And I said to myself, talk about it, quick on the trigger, how did you do it? And my brother was my drummer and he was great. I'd never heard or played with a drummer like him. And he never presumed because of my mother. But I'd be standing in front of that band doing a chorus or something, you know, and he started making faces and cutting them. He was a comedian.
And all of a sudden the band, I had no background.

They were all crying, they were laughing so much. He used to call me Israel. He said I was Jewish, I had Jewish instincts, he meant the money. Then he changed it. I told him to cut it out.
